extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, lawyers, and researchers interested in comparative defamation law
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative summary of how different jurisdictions define, prosecute, and remedy defamation (libel, slander, insult), including statutory elements, defenses, penalties, and special rules for online publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: General definition of defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as "the allegation or [the] allocation of a fact that damages the honor or reputation of the person or body to which the fact is imputed". "A defamatory allegation is considered an insult if it does not include any facts or if the claimed facts cannot be verified."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the baseline element: an imputation of fact that harms reputation; distinguishes 'insult' where no verifiable facts are alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Germany — statutory offences and sections
rubrics_metrics.description: In German law, there is no distinction between libel and slander. Relevant offences include §90 (denigration of the Federal President), §90a (denigration of the State and its symbols), §90b (unconstitutional denigration of the organs of the Constitution), §185 ("insult"), §186 (defamation of character), §187 (defamation with deliberate untruths), §188 (political defamation), §189 (denigration of a deceased person), §192 ("insult" with true statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple tailored offences exist; some provisions treat true statements differently (e.g., §192). Other sections govern procedures, proofs, and exceptions (e.g., §190–§200).

rubrics_metrics.name: India — criminal and civil options; Section 499 and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In India, a defamation case can be filed under either criminal law or civil law. Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code (now replaced by Section 356 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) defines defamation and provides ten valid exceptions. The punishment (Section 500) is simple imprisonment for up to two years, or a fine, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom of speech (Article 19) is subject to "reasonable restrictions" including defamation; criminal prosecutions are complaint-based (CrPC Section 199) and are bailable, non-cognisable, and compoundable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ireland — statute of limitations and reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Defamation Act 2009 the statute of limitations is one year from first publication (may be extended to two years by the courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2009 Act represented significant changes intended to rebalance media freedom and individual reputation compared to prior law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Israel — civil and criminal remedies and thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation can constitute either civil or criminal offence. Civilly, courts may award compensation up to NIS 50,000 without needing proof of material damage. Criminally, defamation is punishable by a year of imprisonment; to constitute a felony it must be intentional and target at least two persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victims need not show pecuniary loss in civil suits; criminal threshold higher (intent, multiplicity of targets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italy — injury vs defamation; press aggravation and professional bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Italy distinguished 'injury' (offending honour in presence — Art. 594) and 'defamation' (offending reputation before many persons — Art. 595). Penalties increase when attribution of a determined fact occurs or when the offence is committed by means of the press or other publicity. Article 31 provides additional penalty for crimes committed with abuse of power or profession, potentially including temporary bans from exercising the profession (affecting journalists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press/publicity aggravates penalties; false accusations can be prosecuted as calunnia (Article 368). Victims could choose to stop criminal prosecution via querela.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japan — civil relief and criminal defamation with public-interest exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilly (Civil Code Art. 723) courts may order measures to restore reputation or compensation. Criminal provisions (e.g., Arts. 230–231) cover defamation and insults; truth is not always a factor in guilt but there is a 'Special Provision for Matters Concerning Public Interest' allowing proof of allegations as a defence. Many defamation offences are prosecuted only upon complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal guilt may be independent of truth except where public interest provisions permit truth as defense; procedural rules (prosecution upon complaint) important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaysia — tort and criminal approach similar to common law
rubrics_metrics.description: In Malaysia, defamation is both a tort and a criminal offence. The principal statutes are the Defamation Act 1957 and the Penal Code; practice follows case law similar to the UK, Singapore, and India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both civil remedies and criminal sanctions available; reliance on common-law principles and precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mexico — abolition in many jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes of calumny, defamation and slanderous allegation (injurias) have been abolished in the Federal Penal Code and in fifteen states; they remain in the penal codes of seventeen states with penalties averaging 1.1 to 3.8 years in jail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patchwork of decriminalization across federal/state levels; penalties vary where law remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Netherlands — civil correction, rectification, and injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Netherlands defamation is mostly addressed by lodging a civil complaint; Article 167 of book 6 Civil Code allows courts to order publication of a correction, deletion of publication, or rectification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may craft remedies such as correction orders and injunctions; emphasis on civil remedies over criminal prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norway — decriminalization and civil shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically defamation was criminal with prison or fines; under a new Penal Code decided in 2005 and effective 1 October 2015, defamation ceased to be a crime and individuals must pursue civil lawsuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift from criminal sanctions to civil remedies (compensation/injunctions) for reputation harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philippines — Revised Penal Code libel definition and cyberlibel
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 353 defines libel as a public and malicious imputation of a crime or vice tending to dishonor someone. Malice is presumed even if true; exceptions include private communications in course of duty and fair reports 'without comments'. Punishment for libel in writing or similar medium includes imprisonment and fines (Art. 355). The Cybercrime Prevention Act (RA 10175) criminalises electronic libel, punishable with imprisonment from six years and one day to up to twelve years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong criminal penalties including for online publication; constitutional challenges have been raised arguing infringement of freedom of expression and due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poland — definition and media aggravation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation is a crime of accusing someone of conduct that may degrade them in public opinion or expose them to loss of necessary confidence. Penalties include fine, limitation of liberty, and imprisonment up to one year; penalties are more severe when the offence happens through the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media/publicity raises penalties; enhanced sentences for group-targeted insults (nationality, ethnicity, religion) up to three years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portugal — defined crimes and publicity/authority aggravations
rubrics_metrics.description: Portuguese crimes include 'defamation' (art. 180), 'injuries' (art. 181), and 'offence to the memory of a deceased person' (art. 185) with varying prison or fine penalties. Penalties are aggravated with publicity (art.183) and when the victim is an authority (art.184); courts may impose costs to publish the judicial decision (art.189).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicity and status of the victim (authority) increase penalties; remedies can include publication of court decision at defendant's expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romania — decriminalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2014, defamation is no longer criminalized in Romania.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms moved defamation disputes out of criminal law, emphasizing civil pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saudi Arabia — defamation of state/rulers under terrorism legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation of the state, or a past or present ruler, is punishable under terrorism legislation; actions that 'threaten Saudi Arabia's unity, disturb public order, or defame the reputation of the state or the king' are treated as terrorism and can involve detention without counsel for extended periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very broad state-protective provisions with severe procedural consequences; speech against rulers/state tightly restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singapore — Protection from Harassment Act remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Division 2 of Part 3 of the Protection from Harassment Act 2014 provides for Stop Publication Order (requiring tortfeasor to stop making the defamatory statement), Correction Order (requiring publication of a correction), and Disabling Order (requiring intermediaries to disable access to the statement). The Act addresses speech that causes 'harassment, alarm, or distress' and is distinct from common-law libel and slander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory remedies aimed at online/harassment contexts supplement traditional defamation law; criminal penalties also possible under the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Korea — truth/public interest and severe penalties for false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Both true and false statements can be considered defamation; penalties increase for false statements. Criminal defamation occurs when a public statement damages reputation unless the statement was true and presented solely for the public interest. False allegations can lead to imprisonment (up to seven years) and fines; civil damages are also available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong criminal enforcement for online and public defamation; prosecutors often investigate cyber defamation even without prior complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweden — denigration, gross defamation, and insulting behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Swedish law criminalizes denigration (ärekränkning) and regulates defamation (förtal, Article 1) as pointing out someone as a criminal or providing information intended to cause exposure to disrespect. Article 2 addresses 'gross defamation' with penalties up to two years; Article 3 covers other insulting behaviour with fines or up to six months' prison if gross. It is generally not required that statements are untrue; vilifying intent suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grossness assessed by content and scope of dissemination; exemptions exist under the Freedom of the Press Act for public-interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Switzerland — willful vs non-willful defamation and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful defamation (knowing falsity and intentional ruin of reputation) is punished with up to three years in prison or with a fine (Art. 174–2). Non-willful defamation carries a maximum monetary penalty of 180 daily penalty units (Art. 173–1). Statute of limitations for defaming a deceased or absent person is 30 years after death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mens rea (knowledge of falsity and intent) distinguishes harsher criminal sanctions from lesser monetary penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taiwan — civil remedies, criminal provisions, and constitutional interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil Code provides compensation and measures to restore reputation, and tort rules allow damages for emotional distress (Arts. 18, 19, 184, 195). Criminal Code (Arts. 309–314) distinguishes insults, slander, and libel; truth is a defence except for private matters. Constitutional Court decisions (e.g., J.Y. Interpretation No. 509 and later judgments) have upheld constitutionality of certain provisions while requiring proportionality, imposing burden of proof for actual malice on the prosecutor/accuser, and emphasizing media's higher duty to fact-check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed civil/criminal regime with judicial balancing of free speech and reputation; courts articulate offender's duty to check validity where public matters are concerned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thailand — civil compensation and criminal Sections 326–327
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil and Commercial Code imposes compensation for false assertions injurious to reputation even if the speaker does not know of untruth (with exceptions for rightful interest). Criminal Code Section 326 defines defamation punishable by up to one year imprisonment or fine; Section 327 covers defamation of the family of deceased persons similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both civil and criminal routes exist; criminal charges used in practice to censor journalists and activists.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Kingdom — abolition of criminal libel and public benefit truth defence
rubrics_metrics.description: The United Kingdom abolished criminal libel on 12 January 2010 (Coroners and Justice Act 2009). Historically, truth was a defence in civil libel and under Libel Act 1843 could be used in criminal libel only if publication was for the 'public benefit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern law removed criminal libel, leaving civil defamation frameworks and defences shaped by public-interest considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States — limited criminal defamation; constitutional constraints and protection against foreign libel judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer than half of U.S. states have criminal defamation laws, but applicability is limited by the First Amendment; no federal criminal defamation statutes exist. Federal and state statutes limit enforceability of offshore defamation judgments (SPEECH Act), modeled on New York's 2008 Libel Terrorism Protection Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Amendment jurisprudence (and state variation) heavily constrains criminal defamation; mechanisms exist to shield domestic writers/publishers from foreign libel judgments that would violate U.S. free-speech norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online/cyber defamation — specific statutes and aggravated enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Several jurisdictions have enacted laws or provisions targeting online or electronic defamation (e.g., Philippines' Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, Singapore's Protection from Harassment Act 2014, proposals in South Korea to imprison for online defamation). Online publication often leads to aggravated penalties or special remedies (disabling orders, takedown/correction, extended prison terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online context commonly triggers separate statutory regimes, faster investigations, and specific remedies for intermediaries/platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements common to many jurisdictions — publication, falsity, harm, and intent/malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Common elements across jurisdictions include publication to a third person, an imputation of fact causing reputational harm, considerations of falsity (varies by jurisdiction), and the offender's state of mind (intent, negligence, or actual malice). Some jurisdictions presume malice; others require proof of actual malice for public-figure matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences: truth may be a full defence in some systems (or in public-interest contexts), while others criminalize even true statements in some circumstances; burden of proof and mens rea standards vary widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating circumstances — publicity, media, victim's status, and abuse of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Many systems increase penalties when defamation occurs via media/press/publicity, when the victim is an authority or public official, or when committed with abuse of power or profession (e.g., journalists may face professional bans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public dissemination and the status of the victim are commonly factored into sentencing and remedial orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies — criminal sanctions, civil damages, correction orders, and injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies include criminal punishment (imprisonment/fines), civil compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary loss (including emotional distress), orders to publish corrections or court decisions, injunctions to delete content, and regulatory/professional sanctions (e.g., bans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of remedy depends on jurisdiction and whether defamation is classified as criminal and/or civil; many jurisdictions are shifting toward civil remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural features — complaint requirement, statute of limitations, and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Some offences are prosecuted only upon complaint (e.g., Japan, Taiwan). Statutes of limitations vary (e.g., Ireland one year; Taiwan two years after injury or up to ten years; Sweden has provisions considering scope of dissemination). Burden of proof for actual malice may rest with prosecutor or accuser in some constitutional rulings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural thresholds (timeliness, complaint requirement) and proof burdens significantly affect enforceability and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special protections and public-interest exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jurisdictions provide special defences or exceptions for publications on matters of public interest, fair reports of official proceedings, privileged communications, and 'rightful interests' of the communicator or receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope and availability of public-interest/privileged defenses differ widely; some systems require objectively reasonable grounds to believe allegations true for the defence to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global patterns and decriminalization trend
rubrics_metrics.description: As of 2012, UNESCO/ARTICLE 19 reported 174 countries retained criminal penalties for defamation, with full decriminalization in 21 countries. Several countries in the excerpt (e.g., Romania, Norway, Mexico partly) have moved toward decriminalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a global trend in some regions toward decriminalizing defamation and favoring civil remedies, but many states retain criminal sanctions, especially for online and politically sensitive speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of severe or notable enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include imprisonment and long sentences for online libel in the Philippines (6–12 years under RA 10175), a 4-year prison sentence for a newspaper publisher in Venezuela after a civil action, and Saudi provisions treating defamation of state/rulers under terrorism laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal cases illustrate wide variance in enforcement severity and raise free-speech concerns in some jurisdictions.
